Punctually at seven o'clock, having scrubbed the ink from my hands and changed into my best, albeit somewhat worn, Sunday suit, I presented myself at the side door of Mr. Gladstone's residence, which adjoined the printing works. The study into which I was shown was a world away from the noisy, ink-stained press-room; it was a sanctuary of quiet learning, lined from floor to ceiling with books on every conceivable subject, the air thick with the pleasant aroma of old leather and pipe tobacco. A cheerful fire crackled in the grate, casting dancing shadows on the walls and glinting off the crystal decanters on a small side-table.

"Ah, Davies, come in, come in, my boy!" said Mr. Gladstone, rising from a great wing-backed chair. "Don't stand on ceremony. Pour yourself a glass of sherry; you've earned it today."

We spent the first hour poring over the proofs of the architectural plates, and I was gratified to see his face light up with genuine pleasure at the sharpness of the lines and the evenness of the impression. He spoke not as a master to a workman, but as one enthusiast to another, discussing the particular challenges of rendering the fine cross-hatching and the subtle gradations of shadow required by the intricate designs.

"It is a thing of beauty, Davies," he said, holding a sheet up to the light. "In our trade, we are not merely mechanics; we are artists and scholars in our own right. We bring light to the world, quite literally. Never forget that. The quality of a man's soul can be seen in the quality of his work."

His conversation then drifted from the specifics of our trade to broader topics. He spoke of the great changes sweeping through London, of the new railways and factories, and of the insatiable hunger for knowledge and printed matter that these changes had created. He told me of his own start in the business, as a poor boy apprenticed to a harsh master in a Fleet Street alley, and of his resolution, even then, to master every aspect of the craft, from cutting his own type to binding the finished books.

"The old guard, like Ackley," he said, and it was the first time he had mentioned the foreman by name, "they see these new presses, these new methods, as a threat. They are comfortable in their old ways and fear what they do not understand. They believe that craft lies only in the sweat of their brow and the strength of their arm. But you, Davies, you understand that the truest craft lies here," he said, tapping his temple with a forefinger, "in the mind. In study, in application, in the constant desire to improve. That is where the future of our trade lies, and you, my lad, are part of that future."

His words filled me with a sense of purpose and pride that was more intoxicating than any sherry. I felt that I was no longer merely a pressman, but a soldier in the army of progress, with Mr. Gladstone as my general. When I finally took my leave of him late that evening, I walked back to my lodgings not on the grimy cobblestones of London, but on air.

While before my colleagues had treated me with a measure of indifferent fellowship, I was now met with suspicious glances and muttered conversations that fell silent whenever I drew near. Ackley, for his part, affected an air of exaggerated civility towards me that was more unnerving than his open hostility. He no longer grumbled or sneered, but instead assigned me my tasks with a tight-lipped smile, calling me "Mister Davies" in a tone laden with mocking respect.

He took to giving me all the most tedious and thankless jobs in the shop: cleaning the accumulated grime from the oldest, disused presses; sorting vast piles of pied type; and fetching and carrying for the other men. "You're making a rod for your own back, lad," he said in a low voice, not looking at me but at the floor. "Doing your duty is all well and good, but with a gaffer like Ackley, it ain't enough. He don't like a man who works hard; he likes a man who knows his place."

"I know my place, Mr. Hemlock," I replied, a little stiffly. "It's to do the work I'm given to the best of my ability."

"Aye, and that's just the trouble," he said, with a dry chuckle. "You're showing him up, see? You'll have to do more'n that. Like most of 'em bully-boys, if you don't bow and scrape a bit, and purtend he's the cleverest man in the room, he's sure to keep you on the rack."

"A skilled operator has a devil of a time in a print shop if he don't know how to grease the wheels with the foreman! They required a large number of funeral announcement cards, of the highest quality, to be delivered by the following morning. The job specified a heavy, black-bordered stock with the text printed in a deep, lustrous black, and a small, intricate silver cross embossed at the top of each card. It was a delicate and expensive job, one which Mr. Gladstone would take great pride in.

Ackley, with a crocodile's smile, assigned the task to me. "Here you are, Mister Davies," he said, loud enough for all to hear. "A job worthy of your particular talents. The master will be wanting to see this one personally. Don't you let him down, now."

I opened it to find it filled, not with the delicate squares of shimmering metal, but with common workshop dust and shavings.

The pigment was still there; it was only the oil that had dried out. Perhaps it could be reconstituted.

We had no such powder, but I spied a roll of tinfoil, which the men used to wrap their bread and cheese in. It was a long shot, but I had no other choice.

I took a sheet of the foil and, using the flat of a steel mallet and a polished block of stone, I began to hammer it. I hammered and hammered, folding it over and hammering again, until the foil was as thin as tissue paper. Then, taking a fine file, I began to scrape the thinned foil, producing a tiny pile of glittering, silvery dust. It was a pittance, but it might be enough. I mixed this dust with a small amount of quick-drying varnish to create a thick, metallic paste.

The other men had stopped their work to watch my strange preparations, murmuring amongst themselves. Ackley stood with his arms crossed, his smug expression slowly turning to one of wary confusion. He had expected me to give up, to come to him beaten, but he had not counted on my resourcefulness.

With my makeshift materials ready, I began the printing. Each card was a trial. I inked the type with my reconstituted ink, made the impression, then, while the ink was still wet, I carefully applied a tiny dab of my silver paste to the embossing die and stamped the cross at the head of the card. The result was not as perfect as it would have been with the proper materials, but it was astonishingly close. The black was deep and solemn, and the silver cross shone with a soft, respectful lustre.

I worked through the night, a silent, grim race against the dawn. Shaw, the night foreman, came and stood by my bench for a long time, watching me work with a quiet intensity. He said nothing, but before he left, he placed a steaming mug of hot tea by my elbow, a silent gesture of solidarity that meant more to me than any words.

Just as the first grey light of morning was filtering through the high, grimy windows of the workshop, I finished the last card. I stacked the entire run, neat and perfect, in a box just as Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Ackley arrived to begin the day's work.

"Well, Davies," Ackley began, his voice dripping with false concern, "I'm afraid I have some bad news for the master. It seems our supplies were not in order, and the funeral cards..."

He trailed off as I held up one of the finished cards for him to see. His jaw dropped. He took the card from my hand, turning it over and over, his eyes wide with disbelief.

Mr. Gladstone stepped forward. "What is this, Ackley? What is the problem?"

"There is no problem, sir," I said, my voice steady despite my exhaustion. "The cards are ready."

Mr. Gladstone took one and examined it closely, a slow smile spreading across his face. He looked at the deep black, at the shining cross, and then he looked at me, a new level of respect in his eyes.

"Why, Ackley," he said, turning to the stunned foreman, "the boy's done it. And with a finer lustre than I've seen from our usual stock! Davies is a better master of the craft than you are!"

This, you may be certain, was the last straw for the foreman, who muttered something about "trickery" and "wasting good tinfoil." But Mr. Gladstone would not hear it. "Nonsense, Ackley," he snapped, "this isn't trickery; it's genius! It's the sort of thinking that built this business, and the sort of thinking that will keep it ahead of the competition." Then, turning to me, his voice softened. "You get some rest, my lad," he said, placing a hand on my shoulder. "You'll find a bonus in your pay this week. You have saved the reputation of this house, and I shall not forget it."

Ackley's face was a mask of pure hatred, a look so venomous it could have curdled milk. As Mr. Gladstone led me towards his office to take my full report, I knew that I had not merely won a skirmish; I had declared war. And I had no doubt that Mr. Ackley would be plotting a new, and far more dangerous, form of revenge.

It started yesterday, just a bit, but it's worse today." I went to the scuttlebutt myself and drew a pannikin. The water was brackish and had a faint, unpleasant chemical taste. I remembered the clean, fresh water we had taken on at the start of our voyage; this was nothing like it. A cold knot of apprehension tightened in my stomach. Sickness at sea was a terrible thing, capable of crippling a ship faster than any storm. The next day, three men were unable to stand their watch, laid up in their bunks with fever and severe stomach cramps. Pat Doolan, who was usually the soul of good cheer, looked pale and worried. "It's a bad business, Mister Leigh," he said, shaking his head. "A very bad business. I've seen the like of it once before, on a ship out of Calcutta. It went through the crew like a fire." Captain Billings convened a conference in his cabin with Mr Ohlsen and me. His face was grave, the lines around his eyes etched deeper than usual. "It's the water," he said, confirming our fears. "I've examined the casks in the main hold. Two of them have been tampered with. The bungs have been loosened and something has been put in them." My mind flew at once to the confined mate and his fawning ally. "The steward, sir," I said. "Williams. He has the keys to the stores." The captain nodded grimly. "And he's the only one who has had contact with Mr Macdougall. It is a plot of such devilish cruelty I can scarcely credit it; to poison the ship's water and disable the crew. Ohlsen, I want you to take two reliable men and place the steward under arrest. Search his belongings and the galley thoroughly." Mr Ohlsen, his ruddy face set like stone, departed to carry out his orders. Captain Billings then turned to me. "Mister Leigh, we are in a precarious position. We have limited fresh water left, and a growing number of sick men. We must find a port, and quickly. Bring me the charts. We must determine our nearest landfall." We bent over the charts together, the great expanse of the South Atlantic spreading out before us. Our position, which I had calculated that very noon, put us hundreds of miles from the regular shipping lanes, and even further from any friendly port. The nearest land was the remote and inhospitable island of Trinidade, a volcanic rock frequented only by sea-birds. "It is our only chance," the captain decided, his finger jabbing at the tiny speck on the chart. "We'll turn the ship and make for it. There may be fresh water there. There has to be." Just then, Mr Ohlsen returned, his expression thunderous. He was holding a small, brown glass bottle. "We found this in the steward's mattress, Captain," he said, placing it on the table. "And we found him trying to dispose of a second one over the side." The captain picked up the bottle and uncorked it, sniffing cautiously at the contents. "Carbolic," he said, his voice hard. "Not enough to kill a man outright in such dilution, but enough to make him wretchedly sick. It is a slow, cowardly poison. Where is Williams now?" "Locked in the carpenter's shop, sir," Ohlsen replied. "And a good thing, too. The men were ready to tear him limb from limb." "And Macdougall?" "He's hammering on his door, sir, shouting for the steward. He knows the game is up." "Let him shout," the captain said with cold fury. "He will have his day of reckoning, I promise you. For now, our priority is the ship and the crew. Mr Ohlsen, you have the conn. Alter course for Trinidade. Mister Leigh, you will be in charge of rationing the clean water. Jorrocks will assist you. We have four casks of the captain's private stock in the lazarette; we will use those for the sick men and for cooking. God willing, it will be enough to see us through." The next few days were a living nightmare. The sickness spread through the ship until nearly half the crew was incapacitated. The healthy men, led by Captain Billings and Mr Ohlsen, worked themselves to the point of exhaustion, standing double watches and tending to their sick shipmates. I found myself in a position of immense responsibility, doling out the precious water, drop by drop, and trying to keep up the spirits of the suffering men. Jorrocks was my shadow, his quiet strength and practical wisdom a constant source of support. Pat Doolan, though weakened himself, refused to leave his galley, brewing thin, nourishing broths for the invalids. Through it all, the _Esmeralda_ ploughed on through the vast, empty ocean, a wounded creature crawling towards a sliver of hope. From Macdougall's cabin, there was only silence now. The initial furious shouting had given way to a sullen, unnerving quiet. The steward, locked away and guarded, was a broken man, weeping and protesting his innocence to anyone who would listen, though none did. The blame for our plight rested squarely on the shoulders of the former first mate, and the hatred for him on board was a palpable thing, thicker than the tropical heat. On the fifth day, a cry came from the lookout at the masthead: "Land ho!" I scrambled up the ratlines myself, my heart pounding, and there it was: a dark, jagged peak rising from the shimmering blue of the sea. It was Trinidade. As we drew closer, however, our hopes began to fade. The island was a forbidding mass of black volcanic rock, pounded by a relentless surf. There were no beaches, no welcoming coves; only sheer cliffs that rose hundreds of feet from the churning water. We circumnavigated the island, our eyes straining for any sign of a fresh water source, a stream, a waterfall, anything. There was nothing. The island was as barren and dry as a cinder. Despair, cold and absolute, settled over the ship. We were so close, yet the life-giving water was still beyond our reach. Captain Billings stood on the poop deck, his telescope trained on the cliffs, his face a mask of grim determination. "There must be a way," he muttered, more to himself than to me. "In an island this size, there must be a catchment, a pool in the crater." "But how could we reach it, sir?" I asked. "The cliffs are impossible to scale." "Not for a seaman," the captain said, a strange light coming into his eyes. He turned and scanned the deck, his gaze falling upon the dejected huddle of the crew. "We will send a party ashore." It was a desperate, almost suicidal plan. A boat would be dashed to pieces against the rocks. But we were a desperate crew. As the captain explained his idea, a grim resolve began to replace the despair. A kedge anchor would be taken by a small, hand-picked crew in the longboat. They would row as close as they dared, and then one man would have to swim through the surf with a light line, find a handhold, and scale the cliff to a high ledge. Once there, he could haul up a heavier rope, and then the anchor itself. With the anchor secured, we could rig a bosun's chair and haul men and water casks up and down from the ship. It was a feat of seamanship worthy of a legend, and it hinged on the courage and skill of one man. Every eye turned to me. I was young, I was fit, and I was the best swimmer on board, having spent my boyhood by the sea. I was also, by a strange turn of fate, the third officer. The choice was mine. "I'll do it, sir," I said, my voice sounding clearer and steadier than I felt. A murmur of approval went through the men. Jorrocks clapped me on the back, his weathered face filled with a mixture of pride and anxiety. "I knew you had it in you, lad," he said hoarsely. "Be careful, now. That surf is a killer." The longboat was lowered, manned by Mr Ohlsen and four of the strongest remaining hands. I stripped to my trousers, a coil of light line slung over my shoulder and the end tied securely around my waist. Captain Billings gave me my final instructions. "Don't fight the sea, Mister Leigh," he said, his hand on my shoulder. "Use its power. Watch the swells. There is a pattern to them. Find your moment, and go. The lives of this crew are in your hands." As the longboat pulled away from the _Esmeralda_, I looked back at the ship. She looked battered and weary, a hospital ship adrift in an empty world. I saw the pale faces of the sick men who had been carried on deck to watch, and I saw the grim, hopeful expressions of the others. And then I saw another face, one I had not seen for days. Framed in the porthole of his cabin prison, was the face of Mr Macdougall. He was watching me, his expression unreadable, a ghost at this terrible feast of our own making. I held his gaze for a moment, then turned away, focusing on the thundering wall of water and rock that lay ahead. My personal war with the Scotsman was a thing of the past; this was a war against the sea itself, for the survival of us all.
